Demorare nouissima tua: et ineternū non peccabis; Nihil sic hoīem a vanita¬ tibus mūdi r̓euocat nihil desideria carnis mortificat: sicut frequēs et intenta meditatio mortis. Facile cōtemnit mundū: qͥ semp̄ se cogitat moriturū. Vinc salomon mo¬ tus ex cōsideratione certissime mortis ait. Risum reputan¬ ui errorē: et gaudio dixi. Quid frustra deciperis? Idcir¬ co melius est ire ad domū luctus: qͣꝫ ad domū cōuiuj. In illa em̄ homo de fine suo redditur sollicitus: in ista ve¬ ro nihil de morte cogitar̉. Quid si hō multis annis vixe¬ rit sup̄ terrā? Quid si diues. si potens. si nobilis fuerit? Mors auctoritatē terrene potestatis nō metuit; diuici¬ as nō attendit: nobilitatem generis nō pauescit. Pari in om̄es fertur vindicta: rapere om̄es sine ꝑsonaꝝ acceptio¬ ne didicit: parcere nulli nouit. Om̄es morimur: oēs ad tribunal christi ꝓ meritis discutiēdis ꝑtrahimur: mane¬ re diu in hoc mūdo nulli cōceditur. ... you receive under your [governance?]: for so many sheep you will answer at the last judgment. Indeed, you are to render an account to God not only for your own soul, but, placed as ruler over all those subject to you, you will answer to God for the souls of each one. O if you now set that day before the eyes of your mind; O if you foresaw your last things, you would easily despise the world with its vain honors. Behold, death hastens; behold, the end approaches; behold, the consummation of your rule hurries on. Therefore, if you are wise, if you fear the peril of your soul, remember past sins, and let the recollection of death never withdraw from your inmost parts. For the wise man says: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. Nothing so recalls a man from the vanities of the world, nothing mortifies the desires of the flesh, as frequent and intent meditation on death. He easily despises the world who always thinks that he is going to die. Hence Solomon, moved by consideration of most certain death, says: I accounted laughter error, and to joy I said: Why are you deceived in vain? Therefore it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting. For in the former a man is made solicitous about his end; in the latter, however, nothing is thought about death. What if a man has lived many years upon the earth? What if he has been rich, powerful, noble? Death does not fear the authority of earthly power; it does not regard riches; it does not dread nobility of birth. With equal vengeance it is borne against all; it has learned to seize all without respect of persons; it knows how to spare none. We all die; we are all dragged before the tribunal of Christ for our merits to be examined; to remain long in this world is granted to no one. Therefore let no one deceive himself; let no one presume upon the honors of the world; let no one trust in the multitude of riches. Let each one prepare himself to die well through a good life; let no one place uncertain hope in length of life, because the longer anyone has lived in the world, the less willing he will be to die. Why is this? Indeed, while life is prolonged, guilt also increases in many things. For often one who, as a young man, is seen prepared and willing to die is found, as an old man, unprepared and most desirous of a longer life. With life grows the appetite for living, and the more a man hastens toward death, the more he loves life. For a young man fears death less, because he knows that he has sinned in fewer things. But when a man’s age is extended to old age, it is defiled by many vices and sins, and he fears death with such anxiety in proportion as he recognizes that he has sinned in many things. Human weakness is prone to sin; and the time of life granted to it, which it ought to have spent in good works, it sees that it has very often indulged in the pleasures of the flesh. A man demands that his life be prolonged for him; and while he delays doing penance for past things, he fears to die unprepared. The wretched man desires to live long in the world, and the longer he is permitted to remain in this life, the less he is found to have amended his ways. He desires to be old, but refuses to be called old. He asks to come to old age through many years, and when he has arrived, he is afraid to depart from the body. O most wretched condition of human weakness. Why are you deceived in vain, mortal man? How long will you not acknowledge that you are going to die? You live badly, and for that reason you are afraid to die. You were unwilling to wipe away the faults of your youth through penance; you did not fear to add sins; and therefore you flee to appear before the eternal judge. But you fear in vain; in vain you are afraid: you will not be able to escape death. You demand that time for repentance be extended for you, and however much prolongation you receive, you do not amend your life. What profit is the longest life to you, when it grows wholly old in sins? What are many years, empty of good works? O rare amendment of life in the aged. Old age always joins new vices to old ones; it always advances into worse things; ever uncertain, it tends toward death. For the disposition that it once put on in adolescence it does not lay aside on any of the days on which it dwells upon the earth. For it is very difficult to leave what one is accustomed to and to think new things with an old mind. What a man learned as a young man, he will retain as an old man. The purpose of amendment, when by delaying one neglects it, one shamefully loses. Behold, while we are healthy we put off saving penance; we postpone the amendment of our life from day to day; and while we desire to live longer in the world, overtaken by the hour of death, we depart from this life without repentance. We have turned over in our mind daily the purpose of amendment; we think of beginning tomorrow; but while we neglect to do violence to ourselves against evil custom, always in

peccatis ꝑseueramus: Nemo em̄ surgere de praua cōsue¬ tudine poterit: nisi qui sibi vim contra desideria carnis fa¬ cit. Hinc de pharaone in exodo dicitur. Induratū est cor pharaonis: nō vult dimittere populū meū: nisi in manu forti et brachio extento. Quis ꝑ pharaonē nisi diabolus accipitur: qui peccatores induros teniere in sua seruitu¬ te ꝑhibetur? Ip̄e em̄ omniū iniquoꝝ caput. quē in luto praue cōsuetudinis suo imperio semel subdiderit: ad peni¬ tentie remedia cōfugere. nisi in manu valida nō ꝑmittit; Que manus valida? Qđ brachiū extentū? Audi. Manus valida gratiā dei omnipotentis exprimit: sine cuius auxilio ad penitentiā nemo resurgit. Enim vero qͥ sua spon¬ te in peccati foueam semel ceciderit: surgere sine speciali gratia dei nō valebit. Stare ante ruinā nemo potest. nisi omnipotentis gratia eū seruādo p̄ueniat: surgere post rui¬ nam nemo potest: nisi misericordis dei clémētia eū iuuā¬ do erigat. Quid ergo liberū arbitriū? Quid brachiū ex¬ tentū? Audi. Libertas arbitrij ad omne opus bonū ne¬ cessaria est: ꝑ quā dei gratia in nobis operatur et velle et ꝑficere pro bona voluntate. Sicut artifex opus suū per¬ instrumentū aptū operatur et ꝑficit: sic gratia dei ꝑ libe¬ rum arbitriū bonū opus in hoībus disponit et facit. Et sicut liberū arbitriū sine gratia dei nihil proficit: ita gra¬ tia dei ad operandū bonū in nobis nostrū arbitrium re¬ quirit. Hinc sanctus apostolus scribens corinthijs dicit. Hortamur vos ne in vacuū gratiā recipitur. Ergo, gratia dei aliquādo in vacuū recipitur? Plane in vacuū; Quomodo hoc? Audi. Quisquis penitentiā sanus age¬ re negligit: quisquis bonū operari dū potest spernit: in vacuū dei gratiā accepit. Idcirco dicitur. Non dimittet populū meū nisi in manu valida et brachio extento: id est in gratia dei in promptu est. Extende ne et gratiā simulet tempus penitentie amittas. Quid moraris? Quid tar¬ das? Quid vim patitur? Quousqꝫ dissimulas? Quousqꝫ del gratiā in vacuū recipis? Cur manū validā ad libera¬tionē tui non ponderas? Quare brachiuni volūtatis tuead gratiā dei vltro se offerentē non extendis? Quare vo¬canti deo non occurris? Quid negligis? Nulla sine labore virtus: nulla cōtra malā consuetudinē sine maximo su¬dore certamina. Ad celeste regnū non venitur ꝑ desideriacarnis sed spūs. Carnis autē desideria nemo potest extinguere: nisi qui gratia dei adiutus vim sibi nouerit inferre. Quā vim! Audi a dn̄io. Qui vult inquit venire postme: abneget semetip̄m sibi. et tollat crucē suā: et sequaturme. Hic latet vis: hic neruus victorie consistit. Si victacarne ad regnū celoꝝ venire desideras: voluntatē ꝓpriamꝓ dei amore contemnas. Ambula secundū spiritū: et carnis desideria superabis. Uerūtamen in omībus his crucētuā ferre quotidie non negligas: si venire postdn̄m salubriter optas. Quā crucē? Quotidiane tentationis. Quonā modo ferenda est? Per patientiā. Ip̄e em̄ dn̄s dicitimitatoribus suis. Et sanctus apl̕us: Patientia inquit vobis necessaria est. Nūc itaqƺ arbitrij tui extendē brachiū: si cupis te¬nebrosum euadere egiptum. Quid formidas? Quid hesitas? Quid dubitas? Quare nō hodie incipis penitentiā:qui te breui moriturū nō ignoras? Ecce iā properat amputatrix penitentie mors: que et vitā tuā et diu dilatū penitendi propositū pariter extinguet. ¶ De mortis amaritudine et iudicij districzione. <Emphasis type="colored">Cap̄. ix.</Emphasis> O Anium terribiliū terribiliū est mors: que cū maximis doloribuscarnem animā rapit de corpore: que in puluerē spiritū ꝓ meritis iudicandū ad tribunal del trāsmittit. Iustus em̄ quacūqƺ morte p̄occupatus fuerit: in refrigerio erit. Nō sic impij nō sic: quibzmors vite pn̄tis dat terminū: et eterne calamitatis iniciū </Emphasis>

in sins we persist: for no one will be able to rise from a depraved habit unless he does violence to himself against the desires of the flesh. Hence it is said of Pharaoh in Exodus: The heart of Pharaoh has been hardened; he does not wish to let my people go except by a strong hand and an outstretched arm. Who is understood by Pharaoh except the devil, who is said to hold hardened sinners in his servitude? For he is the head of all the wicked. Whoever he has once subjected to his rule in the mire of depraved habit, he does not permit to flee to the remedies of penitence except by a strong hand.

What is the strong hand? What is the outstretched arm? Listen. The strong hand signifies the grace of almighty God, without whose aid no one rises again to penitence. For truly, one who has once fallen of his own accord into the pit of sin will not be able to rise without the special grace of God. No one can stand before a fall unless the grace of the Almighty, by preserving him, goes before him; no one can rise after a fall unless the clemency of the merciful God, by helping him, raises him up.

What then is free will? What is the outstretched arm? Listen. Freedom of will is necessary for every good work; through it the grace of God works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to good will. As an artisan works and completes his work through a suitable instrument, so the grace of God through free will disposes and does a good work in human beings. And as free will without the grace of God accomplishes nothing, so the grace of God, for working good in us, requires our will. Hence the holy Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: We exhort you not to receive grace in vain.

Is the grace of God, then, sometimes received in vain? Plainly in vain. How is this? Listen. Whoever, while in health, neglects to do penance; whoever scorns doing good while he can, has received the grace of God in vain. Therefore it is said: He will not let my people go except by a strong hand and an outstretched arm; that is, the grace of God is at hand. Stretch [it] out, lest you lose both grace and [at the same time] the time for penitence. Why do you delay? Why do you tarry? What is suffering violence? How long will you dissemble? How long will you receive the grace of God in vain? Why do you not take account of the strong hand for your liberation? Why do you not stretch out the arm of your will toward the grace of God, which offers itself freely? Why do you not run to meet God as he calls? Why are you negligent?

There is no virtue without labor, no struggle against evil habit without very great sweat. One does not come to the heavenly kingdom by the desires of the flesh, but of the spirit. No one, however, can extinguish the desires of the flesh unless, aided by the grace of God, he has learned to do violence to himself. What violence? Hear it from the Lord. Whoever wishes, he says, to come after me, let him deny himself to himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. Here violence lies hidden; here consists the sinew of victory. If, with the flesh conquered, you desire to come to the kingdom of heaven, you must despise your own will for the love of God. Walk according to the spirit, and you will overcome the desires of the flesh. Nevertheless, in all these things do not neglect to bear your cross daily, if you desire to come after the Lord to your salvation. What cross? That of daily temptation. In what way must it be borne? Through patience. For the Lord himself says to his followers. And the holy Apostle says: Patience is necessary for you.

Now therefore stretch out the arm of your will, if you wish to escape dark Egypt. Why are you afraid? Why do you hesitate? Why do you doubt? Why do you not begin penitence today, since you are not unaware that you will soon die? Behold, death, the cutter-off of penitence, is already hastening; it will extinguish alike your life and your long-deferred purpose of repenting.

On the Bitterness of Death and the Severity of Judgment. Chapter IX.

Of all terrible things death is the more terrible: with the greatest pains it snatches the soul from the body; it [turns] the flesh into dust and sends the spirit, to be judged according to its merits, to the tribunal of God. For the just man, by whatever death he has been overtaken, will be in refreshment. Not so the impious, not so: for them death gives an end to the present life and a beginning to eternal calamity.

Ue peccatoribus obduratis: qꝛ dū penitentiā agere ne¬ gligūt: ad inferos cruciandi sine fine descendūt. Quid iã coͬstitutis intormētis ieħēne terrene ꝓsunt diuicie? Quid breui tꝑe in mūdo habiti honores? Quid gloria mūdi: qͥd regni maięstas? Trāsierūt om̄ia; et sicut fumus euanuerūt? Iacent in tor¬ mentis miseri: ineternū sine fine cruciandi. Ubi sunt vo¬ luptates carnis quas amauerūt? Ubi spes vite lōgioris? Ubi ꝑ tot ānos dilatū penitēdi ꝓpositū? Voluptas in pe¬ nā sine fine duraturā mutata est: spes in cōfusionē: volupta¬ tes in opprobriū. Iā quasi nihil cōfessio perijt a mortuo: penitētie ꝓpositū euanuit: operādi tēpus exspirauit. Bea¬ tus hō qͥ semꝑ est pauidus: qͥ mortis amaritudinē quotibꝰ die p̄ueniendo cogitat: qͥ se ꝑ penitentiā in occursum dei parat. Nihil em̄ sic mentē ad cōpunctionē incitat: nihil sic desideria carnis mortificat: nihil sic penitentiā accele¬ rat: sicut frequens et intenta meditatio mortis. Sic eze¬ chias rex iuda nūcio mortis accepto cōuersus ad parietē fleuit: et dilationē yite lachrymis impetrauit. Sic ninie¬ uite audita communione dn̄ica de vrbis subuersione ti¬ muerūt: cōpunctiqꝫ salubriter in cilicio et puluere peniten¬ tiā agere festinariūt: et veniā a dn̄o cū salute ciuitatis ac¬ ceperūt. Sic achab rex isrl̓ accepta sententia mortis de¬ misso capite in terrā hūiliatus est: qͥ prius elatus et super¬ bus helie sermones cōtemserat. Nemo adeo ferus et suꝑ¬ bus est: qͥ nō mansuescat ad intentā memoriā mortis. Id¬ circo memor esto semꝑ exitus tui ꝯpt non obliuiscaris ex¬ tremi iudicij: si vanas cupis peruincere libidines mūdi. Enīuero qui mortē sibi eviciuo imminere cogitat: nihil in mūdo caducū amat. Memoria siquidē mortis sedula¬ mūdū despicit: carnis incēdia spernit: diuicias cōtemnit. Facile nāqꝫ animus ad cōtemptū terrenoꝝ inducit̉: si de¬ vicina morte sollicite meditet̉. Deniqꝫ si pericula mortis di¬ ligēter attēdimꝰ: mirū sia lachrymis cōtineamꝰ. Tāto em̄ acrius in p̄nicieni nr̄aꝫ diabolus in mortis hora ꝑstrepit: qͣꝫto sibi post hācoēm vincēdi materiā intercipi cognoscit. Scit em̄ infidus humane salutis ꝑsequutor premiū a fi¬ne laboris dependere: et ideo conatur in mortis articulo fortius obsistere: ne homo in sancto ꝓposito possit ꝑ manere. Et ideo multos inter sanctos mortem valde timuisse legimus? eo qꝫ salutis summā in fine consisterenō dubitarent. Quid nos miseri peccatores in illa hora sumus facturi: vbi tremūt sancti et ꝑfecti? Quid facient tabule: vbi magne domus quassantur colūne? Si mortem iustus metuit: impius et peccator quomodo stabūt? Uenobis. Penitentie tempus male expendimus: et tanqͣꝫ securi ad mortē ꝓperamus Decipitur: qui mortē sine penitentiā prestolatur; Qui male viuit: nunqͣꝫ sine penitentia bene moritur; Pendente in cruce dn̄o salutis insidiator affuisse legitur: et qui nullū in eo peccatū vnqͣꝫ inuenire potuit: suū quesitus in morte aliqd accessit. Quis modo non timeat: si callidi hostis versuciam pensat? Nonrienti quondā sanctiffimo p̄sule thuronoꝝ martino diabolus affuit: et suū in eo aliquid quesuit. Tui sanctus. Quid hic stas cruenta bestia? Quē expectas Discede: nihil in me funeste reperies; Ad hec diabolus indignās respondisse fertur. Morienti filio dei in cruce affui: et tibi aꝑproplare non debeo? Nemo vncꝗ mortuus est: cui morienti non fuerim presens. Hinc sancti viricū de omnibus semper diuina iudicia ꝑtimescant. tunc tamen vehementer metuūt: cum ad soluendum humane cōditionis debitū adueniēti districto iudici propinquare secernūt: et fit tanto timor acrior: quanto et retributio eterna vicior. Quid nos miseri vermiculi agere morituri poterimꝰ? Timeamus ergo mortē nobis certiffimo venturā: ne paucamus p̄sentē. Nihil em̄ morte certius: nihil in humanis durius: nihil horribilius. Et cũ de ventura morte omnes simus certifumi: nescimus tn̄ qua hora veniat: vel in quo statu nos prosternat; Vinc in euāgelio dn̄s nos admonet dicens. Uiligilate: quia nescitis diem necꝗ horā. Et inducens super hoc similitudinē ait. Et vos similes hoībꝫ expectantibus

Woe to hardened sinners, who, while they neglect to do penance, descend to hell to be tormented without end. What use are earthly riches now to those set in the torments of Gehenna? What use are honors held in the world for a brief time? What use the glory of the world, what the majesty of a kingdom? All have passed away, and like smoke have vanished. The wretched lie in torments, to be tortured forever without end. Where are the pleasures of the flesh which they loved? Where the hope of a longer life? Where the resolve to repent, postponed through so many years? Pleasure has been changed into punishment that will endure without end; hope into confusion; pleasures into reproach. Now confession has perished from the dead man as though from nothing; the purpose of penance has vanished; the time for working has expired. Blessed is the man who is always fearful, who thinks every day in advance on the bitterness of death, who prepares himself through penance to meet God. For nothing so stirs the mind to compunction, nothing so mortifies the desires of the flesh, nothing so hastens penance, as frequent and intent meditation on death. Thus Hezekiah, king of Judah, when he had received the message of death, turned to the wall and wept, and obtained a postponement of life by tears. Thus the Ninevites, when they heard the Lord’s proclamation concerning the overthrow of the city, were afraid, and, salutarily pierced with compunction, hastened to do penance in sackcloth and ashes, and received pardon from the Lord together with the safety of the city. Thus Ahab, king of Israel, having received the sentence of death, with lowered head was humbled to the ground, who before, exalted and proud, had despised the words of Elijah. No one is so savage and proud that he is not made gentle by intent remembrance of death. Therefore always be mindful of your end, that you may not forget the last judgment, if you desire to overcome the vain lusts of the world. For indeed he who thinks death is threatening him while he is alive loves nothing perishable in the world. The diligent memory of death despises the world, scorns the fires of the flesh, contemns riches. For the soul is easily led to contempt of earthly things if it meditates anxiously on death close at hand. Finally, if we diligently attend to the dangers of death, it is a wonder if we hold back from tears. For the more sharply does the devil make a din in our [unclear] at the hour of death, the more he knows that after this [unclear] the opportunity of conquering is being taken from him.

For that faithless persecutor of human salvation knows that the reward depends upon the end of the labor, and therefore he strives to resist more strongly at the point of death, lest a man be able to remain in his holy purpose. And therefore we read that many among the saints greatly feared death, because they did not doubt that the whole of salvation consisted in the end. What shall we wretched sinners do in that hour, where the holy and perfect tremble? What will boards do where the great columns of a house are shaken? If the righteous man fears death, how will the impious and the sinner stand? Woe to us. We spend the time of penance badly, and, as though secure, hasten toward death. He is deceived who awaits death without penance. He who lives badly never dies well without penance. When the Lord was hanging on the cross, the plotter against salvation is read to have been present; and he who could never find any sin in him sought something of his own in death. Who now would not fear, if he weighs the craftiness of the cunning enemy? When that most holy bishop of Tours, Martin, was once dying, the devil was present and sought something of his own in him. The saint said: “Why do you stand here, bloody beast? Whom do you await? Depart; you will find nothing deadly in me.” To this the devil is said to have answered indignantly: “I was present when the Son of God was dying on the cross, and ought I not to come near you? No one has ever died at whose death I was not present.” Hence, though holy men always fear the divine judgments in all things, nevertheless they are then vehemently afraid when they perceive that they are drawing near to the strict judge as he comes to exact the debt of the human condition; and fear becomes the sharper, the more eternal the recompense of vices is. What will we wretched little worms be able to do when we are about to die? Let us therefore fear death, which will most certainly come to us, lest we [unclear] it when present. For nothing is more certain than death, nothing among human things harsher, nothing more horrible. And although we are all most certain of death to come, yet we do not know at what hour it will come, or in what state it will cast us down. Hence in the Gospel the Lord admonishes us, saying: “Watch, for you know neither the day nor the hour.” And, introducing a similitude on this, he says: “And you, be like men waiting”

envy rages more fiercely, when the final battle is being waged for eternal triumph. But in vain do we fear death, which we cannot escape. Hence the wise man admonishes, saying: “Do not fear the judgment of death.” As if he were saying openly: Do not fear what you cannot escape; nor increase the danger by fearing, lest you fall into despair. What then? Is death therefore not to be feared? It is to be feared by the wicked and the reprobate, for whom it makes an entrance to hell. But by the good and the faithful it is to be feared in such a way that it restrains them from sin, not that it breaks their constancy. Yet for all, discreet meditation on death is good and useful; the memory of it preserves the good and the just in their holy purpose, and calls back the impious and sinners to repentance. For to the holy and the just, death is the entrance to eternal life, as the blessed Apostle says: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Why gain? Because by death a passage is prepared for me to joy; through it I go from labor to rest, from abasement to glory, from poverty to incomparable riches, from fear to security, from the world to heaven, from death to eternal life. But this confidence belongs only to the perfect, to whom this world has been crucified, and they to the world. Unhappy I, Trithemius: who will deliver me from the body of this death? I endure the weariness of the present life, and I greatly fear to die. I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, but I fear to appear before the inward judge, whom I recognize that I have offended by many sins. I bear my sojourn with distress, in which I see that I have made no progress; and therefore with the holy Apostle I mix lamentation. For he says: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish I do not find. For the good that I will, I do not do; but the evil that I do not will.” If the holy Apostle could say this of himself, what shall we wretches do? Woe to us, to whom at times neither to will is present nor to accomplish. O if the strict examination of the inward judge never fled from the eyes of our mind; O if the memory of the last things never withdrew from our thoughts, the world would easily become worthless to us, and the bitterness of repentance would please us. How strictly God judges the sins of men after the deed is shown by many examples. For no sin is so small that a punishment would not have to be assigned for it, if it has not been purged in this life through repentance.

Let us carefully consider what is read concerning the saints of God, Severinus, archbishop of Cologne, and Paschasius, deacon of the Roman Church: that both, shining with miracles, were seen after death in the punishments of purgatory; the one because, occupied with the affairs of the commonwealth, he had at times performed the canonical hours too negligently; the other because in the election of Pope Symmachus he had dissented from the will of others, although with good zeal. What shall we wretches do, if men most holy and renowned for miracles could not escape the punishments of purgatory? What, I say, shall we unjust men do, if saints are tortured after death in the punishments of purgatory? How will the impious man be able to escape punishments, if the saint could not? Therefore let us fear, brothers; by fearing let us take care, lest through negligence we fall. Let us do penance at all times, because in this life alone is penance fruitful, when we can not only escape punishments, but also merit glory.

That, by consideration of death and judgment, the world, the flesh, and all the pleasures of this life are to be despised.

Chapter 10.

Divine Scripture admonishes us, saying: “In all things remember your last things.” And to the sinful nation Moses says: “It is a nation without counsel and without prudence: would that they were wise and understood, and would provide for their last things.” What last things? Those, namely, that follow the present life. What are they? Judgment and death. Indeed, how useful the memory of death is to a man, the wise man declares, saying: “Son, remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Behold, death hastens; the strict judgment of God approaches. How long will you sleep? How long will you put off repentance? You will not be able to live long in this world; you will quickly be snatched to the judgment of God, where you are to receive a sorrowful sentence for the negligence of your life. Therefore now, while you live and are healthy, do penance; amend your life for the better; purge your conscience. Whatever good your hand can do,

[unclear] work, because neither work nor reason, nor wisdom nor knowledge, will exist among the dead, whither you are hastening. Now is the time of penitence; now the days of labor, in which we can redeem our sins through holy exercises and, for small works, obtain the heavenly kingdom. The world passes away, and its desire; men die, and are snatched from our memory as though they had never been. Why do you trust in gold, O rich man? Why do you glory in power? Why do you not consider that you will shortly die? Put down your haughtiness; cast away vain confidence. Death does not fear honors, does not heed riches, does not distinguish age. It is one for all; it spares no one, reverences no one. As with the servant, so also with the lord; it makes the farmer equal to the prince; it equates scepters with mattocks. It renders equal judgment to all, pronounces a just sentence, accepts no person. It does not ask a man’s will; it imposes necessity on all. Whether a man is prepared to die or not, it does not weigh; it hastens to seize him for whom it has come; it gives no consideration to the words of one promising, however great they may be. In all the days in which a man lives upon the earth he hastens toward death, and, as if with eyes closed, blind, he hastens to the pit. No age is secure from death; no time is safe; no place under heaven has immunity. Age does not excuse a man who is to die; time does not free him; place does not preserve him. Since, therefore, at every age, place, and time we are subject to death, let us await it continually prepared, for it watches us at every moment. The doubtful, uncertain, and changeable death of the human condition diligently warns us that, being solicitous about our death, we should nowhere presume vainly. For Scripture says: Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil. Indeed, he who fears the coming of death guards himself from every negligence, so far as human frailty permits, and desires to be found ready in all things. Who is the one who fears death in a salutary way? He who, by fearing, lives well. The wicked fear and dread death, but in fearing they live badly. Fear profits nothing where there is no progress. For the rich of this world greatly fear the dominion of death, because, entangled in earthly desires, they are afraid to depart from this age, since they have loved nothing outside the world. He who is conscious of evil in himself dreads the coming of the judge. Indeed, he who does evil hates the light, fearing the correction of judgment. But what does it profit? Necessity drives us toward death, and human will cannot withstand it. After death judgment is at hand, where conscience will accuse as witness and justice will judge. Therefore, while we live in the flesh, let us prudently fear death; by fearing let us prepare ourselves, because we cannot escape. Let us do penance for past sins; let us beware of future ones; and thereafter let us strive to live in such a way that we may not fear death. A sound conscience always has joy, since it places its hope in the help of the Most High, whose commandments it humbly observes. But salvation is far from sinners, who seek earthly honors, who cultivate greed, who at all times seek the pleasures of the flesh. Deservedly such people fear death, for they do not have the testimony of a good conscience. For just as death is for the good an entrance from poverty to the kingdom, so for the reprobate it is an approach to hell. Blessed is the man who meanwhile is always fearful, who does not love the vanities of the world, who spurns perishable riches, who flees the desires of the flesh, who guards the commandments of God with humble devotion. Such a man awaits death securely, having confidence in the grace of God alone. For no one is holy by his own powers, but God works all things in all, who by his mercy may grant us eternal life. Amen.
